LET'S GET STARTED.

The three main hitch types explained visually. Choose based on your vehicle and priorities.

GOOD: Standard Exposed
Exposed Hitch & Body
Both the receiver tube and main hitch body stick out from the vehicle. Most common and affordable option.
Best for: Trucks, work vehicles, heavy towing, budget-conscious buyers

Brands: Curt, Draw-Tite, Reese

Price: $400-$600 installed

Towing: Up to 20,000 lbs

Tongue Weight: 200-2,000 lbs

Lead time: Usually in stock

BETTER: Concealed Body
Exposed Receiver Only
Only the receiver tube shows. Main hitch body is tucked behind bumper. Much cleaner appearance.
Best for: SUVs, crossovers, better ground clearance, cleaner look

Brands: EcoHitch, Curt select models

Price: $400-700 installed

Towing: 2,000-5,000 lbs

Tongue Weight: 200-500 lbs

Lead time: 1-2 weeks

BEST: Completely Hidden
Invisible When Not In Use
Completely hidden underneath vehicle. Receiver only appears when you slide out a removable panel.
Best for: Luxury vehicles (Audi, BMW, Lexus, Tesla), zero visual impact

Brands: Stealth Hitches

Price: $800-1,200 installed

Towing: 3,500-5,000 lbs

Tongue Weight: 350-500 lbs

Lead time: 1-2 weeks, full-day install

What Most Shops Won't Tell You

The True Weight of Carrying Bikes Off Your Hitch

This is one of the most common mistakes we see from customers who buy a hitch online or at a big-box store. A smaller vehicle gets sold a 1¼-inch receiver because it's cheaper or "good enough." That decision often limits usable tongue weight and can make carrying 2–4 bikes unsafe—especially e-bikes.

When we're planning for multiple bikes, we typically spec a 2-inch receiver because it supports higher tongue weight ratings, a wider rack selection, and better long-term flexibility.

Example: Vehicle tongue weight rating of 250 lbs

Bike rack weight: 90 lbs

4 e-bikes at 60 lbs each: 240 lbs

Total static load: 330 lbs — exceeds the 250 lb rating

That's just static weight. Leverage multiplies the effective load—the farther the weight sits behind the receiver, the harder it pulls on your vehicle's structure. Add road impacts, and the real forces spike well beyond the number on the scale.

Bottom line: We need to know what you're mounting—rack model, number of bikes, bike weights, and your vehicle's ratings—so we can spec the right receiver size, hitch class, and rack configuration safely. A $50 difference in hitch choice can mean the difference between a safe setup and a damaged vehicle.

Wiring 101 — The Critical Upgrade Most People Miss

Your trailer has to communicate with your vehicle—lights, signals, braking. That requires proper wiring.

Bike racks don't require wiring. Trailers do. The most efficient time to add wiring is during the initial hitch install—not later when the vehicle has to be reopened.

Basic: 4-Pin Flat
4-Pin Flat Connector
Basic lighting connection that handles running lights, brake lights, and turn signals. The standard starting point for light-duty towing.
Best for: Small utility trailers, light-duty towing, basic trailer lighting needs

Signals: Running lights, brake lights, turn signals

Cost: Typically $100–$150 installed + parts

Install time: Minimal added time during hitch install

Limitation: No electric brakes, no reverse lights, no aux power

Recommended: 7-Pin Round
7-Pin Round Connector
Everything a 4-pin does plus electric trailer brakes, reverse lights, and auxiliary power. The full-capability option for serious towing.
Best for: RVs, boat trailers, enclosed trailers, anything with brakes

Signals: All 4-pin functions + brakes, reverse, aux power

Cost: Typically $150–300 installed + parts

Install time: Best done during initial hitch install

Our take: Install now—much cheaper than adding later

Brake Controller
Wireless Brake Controller
Required if your trailer has electric brakes (most over ~3,000 lbs do). Synchronizes your vehicle's braking with the trailer for safe, controlled stops.
Best for: Heavy trailers, RVs, boat trailers, any trailer with electric brakes

Proportional: Matches trailer braking to your brake pressure

Cost: Call for quote

Time-delay: Applies preset braking after short delay

Requires: 7-pin wiring connection

Common Questions

Do I need a 1¼" or 2" receiver for my bike rack? For 1-2 bikes: either works. For 3-4 bikes or e-bikes: we strongly recommend 2" receivers due to higher tongue weight ratings and better rack selection. Tell us what you're planning to carry and we'll spec it correctly.

Do I need an appointment? Call ahead recommended: (916) 563-7333. Most days we can do same-day, but summer gets busy.

Will this void my warranty? No. Federal law prohibits manufacturers from voiding warranties for aftermarket parts. We only install hitches engineered for your vehicle.

Which type should I choose? Trucks/heavy towing: standard exposed (GOOD). SUVs wanting cleaner look: concealed body (BETTER). Luxury vehicles/zero visual impact: hidden Stealth (BEST).

How much does it cost? Standard with 4-pin: $200-500. Concealed with 7-pin: $400-700. Stealth hidden: $800-1,200. Add $150-300 for brake controller.

What's your warranty? Our labor guaranteed for life of vehicle ownership. Hitch has manufacturer warranty (typically lifetime metal). Wiring 1-3 years by brand.
